source: Tran and Kiela (2026) Single-Agent LLMs Outperform Multi-Agent Systems on Multi-Hop Reasoning Under Equal Thinking Token Budgets
finding: At equal thinking-token budgets, a single agent matches or beats five multi-agent designs (sequential, subtask-parallel, parallel roles, debate, ensemble) on FRAMES and MuSiQue 4-hop. Multi-agent only wins at the smallest budget or when context is degraded.
numbers: 3 model families (Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B, Gemini 2.5 Flash/Pro). Average accuracy over 8 model-dataset cells: 100 thinking tokens SAS 0.290, debate 0.370, sequential 0.364, ensemble 0.280; 500 tokens SAS 0.390, debate 0.380, ensemble 0.310; 1000 tokens SAS 0.418, debate 0.388, ensemble 0.333; 2000 tokens SAS 0.421 vs debate 0.403 and ensemble 0.372; 5000 tokens SAS 0.427 vs debate 0.420 and ensemble 0.411. Gemini-2.5-Pro FRAMES at high budget: ensemble best.
quote: single-agent systems (SAS) can match or outperform MAS
limits: Multi-hop QA only. LLM judge. Authors report budget-control artifacts in the Gemini API. The ensemble splits the budget across workers that are copies of one model (no heterogeneity).
agent_relevance: Gap 1 for same-model copies: parallel branches cost budget and lose at equal tokens above about 500 thinking tokens. Heterogeneity was not tested, so diversity itself is still open.

finding: When the single agent's context is damaged by deletion, masking, substitution or distractors, the sequential multi-agent system only catches up at heavy damage.
numbers: MuSiQue 4-hop, Qwen3-30B-A3B, 1000 thinking tokens. SAS vs sequential: deletion 0.3: 0.245 vs 0.221; masking 0.7: 0.220 vs 0.231; substitution 0.7: 0.200 vs 0.225; distractors k=10: 0.257 vs 0.228, k=30: 0.256 vs 0.233. Intervals overlap in most rows.
limits: Differences are 1 to 3 points with overlapping bootstrap intervals; one model, one task.
agent_relevance: Splitting work across agents helps only when one agent cannot use its own context well. For our single agent: keep a clean single context plus a few retained alternatives.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) Demystifying Multi-Agent Debate: The Role of Confidence and Diversity
finding: Vanilla debate performs similar to or worse than majority vote. Initial answer diversity correlates (weakly) with debate gain. Selecting a diverse pool of initial answers raises the chance a correct answer is present at the start; confidence-weighted updates beat vote.
numbers: Qwen-2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, 62 datasets incl. 57 MMLU subtasks. Pass@5 at round 0, random vs diversity-selected: Qwen 0.7921 vs 0.9097; Llama 0.7423 vs 0.9026. Unique answers@5: Qwen 1.45 vs 1.61; Llama 1.92 vs 2.32. Higher temperature raised answer diversity little (Qwen gave the same answer in other languages).
quote: vanilla MAD often underperforms simple majority vote despite higher computational cost
limits: Two small open models. Diversity is measured as distinct final answers, not embeddings. Selection needs a larger candidate pool, so compute is not equal to plain majority vote.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: answer-level diversity, not temperature, is what the gain needs. Selecting for distinct answers is a cheap rule for a single scaffold agent that keeps alternatives.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) theory section: debate as martingale, confidence breaks it
finding: Under homogeneous agents and uniform updates, debate preserves expected correctness (martingale). If confidence correlates with correctness, belief becomes a submartingale and drifts to the truth.
numbers: Theorem 1 (submartingale) assumes homogeneous, fully connected agents and confidence positively correlated with correctness. GRPO training used a harder subset (accuracy near 50%) because easy data gave max confidence on everything.
limits: Proof depends on the confidence-correctness assumption, which is weak for verbal confidence in small models.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: mandatory uptake only helps if the critique signal carries information about correctness. Links to calibrated-confidence work in other subfields.

source: Choi, Zhu and Li (2025) Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent LLMs?
finding: Majority voting before any debate accounts for most of the gain usually credited to multi-agent debate. Debate is modelled as a martingale on agent beliefs; mean accuracy across rounds is flat empirically.
numbers: Seven benchmarks; five agents; NeurIPS 2025. An oracle variant that locks correct answers drifts upward; two practical variants (e.g. MAD-Conformist) use the vote as the signal.
quote: Majority Voting alone accounts for most of the performance gains typically attributed to MAD
limits: Homogeneous agents (same model). Theory assumes a Dirichlet-compound-multinomial belief model.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 8: free-form exchange adds little over independent samples plus a vote; only a directional rule (keep correct, bias updates) helps.

source: Wynn, Satija and Hadfield (2025) Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate
finding: With heterogeneous groups (GPT, Llama, Mistral mixes) debate often lowers accuracy over rounds, even when stronger models outnumber weaker ones. More answers flip from correct to incorrect than the reverse, and flipping rises with the number of peers who disagree.
numbers: Tasks CommonsenseQA, MMLU, GSM8K; groups such as 3 same-model, 2+1 mixes and a diverse 1+1+1 team. A correctness-payoff prompt did not reduce correct-to-incorrect flips (sometimes increased them).
quote: debate can lead to a decrease in accuracy over time
limits: Small and mid models (Mistral-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, GPT). Per-cell numbers are only in figures, not read.
agent_relevance: Diversity of model quality without a rule on whom to trust hurts. Gap 8: uptake of critique can be harmful if it means conforming; the rule must be evidence-based.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? Multi-Agent Debate Strategies for LLMs
finding: Multi-agent debate does not reliably beat self-consistency or ensembling of reasoning paths, and Medprompt (no debate) was best and cheaper on medical QA. After hyperparameter tuning, Multi-Persona debate improves.
numbers: MedQA 4-option; cost compared by API calls; best debate setups reached about 61% on MedQA; Medprompt best overall.
limits: ICML 2024; GPT-3.5/GPT-4 era; tuning the agreement level changes the ranking, so debate results are protocol-sensitive.
agent_relevance: Supports 'do not add debate as a state'. The one parameter that mattered was the agreement level, close to the timing question in gap 2.

source: Chen et al. (2026) Diversity Collapse in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: Structural Coupling and Collective Failure in Open-Ended Idea Generation
finding: Over 10,000 research proposals on 20 topics, multi-agent ideation loses diversity through interaction structure: stronger aligned models give less marginal diversity, authority-led groups are less diverse, bigger groups give diminishing returns and dense talk converges early.
numbers: Vendi score agreed with five expert annotators in 87% of pairwise diversity judgments (all three embedding metrics above 80%). Group size N=3 to 7: Vendi rises but Vendi/N falls from 1.03 to 0.47. Horizontal junior-style groups Vendi 8.08; interdisciplinary expert-role groups 4.65 (quality 8.50 vs 7.88 on a 10-point scale). AI-research task baseline Vendi above 2.6. Embeddings: text-embedding-3-large, checked with BGE-large.
quote: diversity collapse arises primarily from the interaction structure rather than inherent model insufficiency
limits: Diversity measured by embeddings, quality by LLM scores. No ground truth for ideas.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: gives measured Vendi values and shows diversity per added agent halves by 7 agents. For parallel branches: few independent branches, no early mutual viewing.

source: Chen et al. (2026) topology experiments: nominal group technique and subgroups
finding: A blind-writing phase before sharing (nominal group technique) starts with the highest semantic diversity; splitting the group into subgroups gives a mid-debate diversity rebound and the most sustained constructive conflict. Both beat the standard open-talk baseline.
numbers: Constructive conflict = interactions with an LLM critique score of 7 or more. Effects shown in figures only (no table value read). Authors say the ranking replicated on GPT-5.1 and in a persona-by-topology factorial.
limits: Measures diversity and conflict, not final correctness. Fixed rounds, fixed temperature.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM test of transient diversity (gap 2): delaying sharing keeps diversity high. Whether it raises accuracy is NOT shown; stays open.

source: Li, Naito and Shirado (2026) Systematic Failures in Collective Reasoning under Distributed Information (HiddenBench)
finding: In hidden-profile tasks LLM groups converge prematurely on shared evidence. A short structured protocol (share facts plus one reason the front-runner may be wrong, then decide) lifts accuracy sharply.
numbers: 65 tasks, 15 LLMs: 30.1% with distributed info vs 80.7% for single agents with full info. Rounds T=5,10,15,20: peak at 15, falls at 20 (post-discussion 0.233 vs full-profile 0.733). Group size N=3 to 7 (GPT-4.1): gain from communication falls from +0.348 to +0.006. Structured protocol (18 tasks, 5 runs, 4 agents): GPT-4.1 0.037 to 0.800; Gemini-2.5-Flash 0.173 to 0.727; Flash-Lite 0.043 to 0.743.
quote: agents cannot recognize or act under latent information asymmetry
limits: Information-pooling task, not search or discovery; small protocol test (18 tasks); very low baselines.
agent_relevance: A forced 'give one reason the leader is wrong' step is a Longino-style uptake rule with a large measured effect (gap 8), but against no protocol, not against free self-critique at equal tokens.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
finding: Taxonomy of 14 failure modes in 3 categories built from 150 traces (kappa 0.88), applied to 1600+ traces from 7 frameworks. Failure rates 41% to 86.7%.
numbers: Category shares: system design 41.8%, inter-agent misalignment 36.9%, task verification 21.3%. Modes: step repetition 15.7%, reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%, not recognising completion 12.4%, disobey task spec 11.8%, incorrect verification 9.1%, incomplete verification 8.2%, task derailment 7.4%, wrong assumptions 6.8%, premature termination 6.2%, ignoring other agents' input 1.9%, withholding info 0.85%.
limits: Shares are of failures found, not of all runs; LLM-as-judge annotates most traces; 2024 frameworks (ChatDev, MetaGPT, AG2).
agent_relevance: Gap 9: about 21 percent of failures are verification, which maps to checking and stopping guardrails. Ignoring peer input is rare (1.9%), so forced uptake targets a small failure mode.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) intervention case studies (Appendix H)
finding: Better roles or an added verification step give gains, but modest and not universal. A verifier's presence does not remove failures because verifiers check superficially.
numbers: ChatDev ProgramDev success: baseline 25.0, improved prompts 34.4 (+9.4), new topology with high-level objective verification 40.6 (+15.6). HumanEval 89.6, 90.3, 91.5. AG2 GSM-Plus GPT-4 84.75 to 89.75 (prompt) and 85.50 (topology); GPT-4o 84.25 to 89.00 and 88.83.
limits: Two systems, intervals about 1.2 to 1.9 points; the paper says interventions are not universal and depend on the LLM.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partly answered: a verifier removes some failures, not the failure rate. A verifier needs an external check (tests, rules) to work.

source: Naik et al. (2024) Diversity of Thought Improves Reasoning Abilities of LLMs (DIV-SE, IDIV-SE)
finding: Model-generated distinct approaches and personas, ensembled over separate calls (DIV-SE) or inside one call (IDIV-SE), beat CoT and self-consistency at similar cost on strong models. Gains vanish on GPT-3.5 for planning.
numbers: GPT-4 zero-shot CoT: Graph colouring CoT 15.0, best SC 23.0, IDIV-SE 74.0, DIV-SE 97.0; Blocksworld 3 CoT 70.0, SC-10 73, IDIV-SE 82, DIV-SE 94; Blocksworld 4/5 CoT 40.0, SC 41.2, IDIV-SE 57, DIV-SE 69.6. AQuA GPT-3.5 ZS: CoT 59.0, SC-5 63.37, IDIV 62.6, DIV 72.83. GPT-3.5 Blocksworld: no gain (6% and 0.6% baselines). GSM8K GPT-4 94/95 to 96.3. Persona plus approach on AQuA-RAT GPT-3.5: 57.48 to 65.75 (+8.27).
limits: No variance or seeds reported (single runs); cost matched by dollar estimate, not exact tokens; needs good instruction following; LLaMA-2 70B zero-shot gain negligible.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: large reported gains but no variance and no independent replication found in this session. Promising, not established.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) When 'A Helpful Assistant' Is Not Really Helpful: Personas in System Prompts Do Not Improve Performance
finding: Across 162 roles and 2,410 factual questions, adding a persona to the system prompt does not improve accuracy over no persona. The best role per question is an upper bound that cannot be predicted: automatic role selection is no better than random.
numbers: 9 open models in 4 families (FLAN-T5-XXL, Llama3 8B and 70B, Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5 3B to 72B); 6 relationship types and 8 domains; in-domain coefficient 0.004 (p<0.01); audience prompts beat speaker prompts with a small effect.
quote: adding personas in system prompts does not improve model performance across a range of questions
limits: Multiple-choice factual questions (MMLU-type), not discovery. Persona acts alone, not inside a debate.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: on objective tasks personas give no reliable gain. Approach diversity (d13) differs from persona flavour. Contrasts with c04 (persona gain in debate, MMLU 71.1 to 74.2).

source: Li et al. (2025) Self-MoA, as re-read in the cross-check pass (not re-opened in the gap pass)
finding: Cross-check correction carried forward: Self-MoA 65.7 vs Li et al.'s own 2-layer mixed MoA 59.1 uses a weaker replication; the original 3-layer MoA reports 65.1.
limits: Taken from critique.md, not re-opened this pass.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: do not cite Self-MoA as beating MoA by 6.6; the baseline was weaker than the original.
